deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT. This page continues a fragment on the question: for a prime q = 2p+1 not dividing a, which of a^p - 1 or a^p + 1 is divisible by q? In modern terms this is Euler's criterion, a^((q-1)/2) ≡ (a/q) (mod q). The rule from the preceding page is that the sign depends only on q mod 4a, and that q ≡ r and q ≡ -r (mod 4a) give the same sign. Once one prime q0 = 2p0+1 with a known sign is found, every prime 2p+1 ≡ ±q0 (mod 4a) has the same sign.

(1) Top lines, case a = 6. On the previous page Euler noted that p = 1 (q = 3) is impossible since 3 | 6. This excludes p ≡ 1 and p ≡ 10 (mod 12), i.e. q ≡ 3 and q ≡ 21 (mod 24), which are multiples of 3. Since 5 | 6^2 - 1, the case p = 2 gives sign +1. The same holds for every prime q = 2p+1 ≡ ±5 (mod 24):
- q ≡ 5 (mod 24) means p ≡ 2 (mod 12), giving the exponents 14, 26, 38, 50, 62, ...
- q ≡ 19 (mod 24) means p ≡ 9 (mod 12), giving 9, 21, 33, 45, 57, ...
Thus 6^p ≡ +1 (mod 2p+1) for these p whenever 2p+1 is prime.

(2) Test 1: is 6^50 ≡ 1 (mod 101)? Euler's method: assume the residue, add a multiple of N to make it divisible by 6, then divide by 6 to lower the exponent.
- 6^50 ≡ 1 ≡ 1 + 101 = 102 = 6·17, so 6^49 ≡ 17.
- 17 - 101 = -84 = -6·14, so 6^48 ≡ -14.
- -14 - 202 = -216 = -6^3, so 6^45 ≡ -1.
- [Implicit step, mine:] dividing 6^50 ≡ 1 by 6^45 ≡ -1 gives 6^5 ≡ -1.
- -1 - 101 = -102 = -6·17, so 6^4 ≡ -17.
- -17 + 101 = 84 = 6·14, so 6^3 ≡ 14.
- [Implicit, mine:] 6 = 6^6/6^5 ≡ -(6^3)^2 ≡ -196 ≡ -196 + 202 = 6. This is a true identity, so the assumed residue is consistent: 'quod quia est verum, patet regula'.
Direct check: 6^2 = 36; 6^3 = 216 ≡ 14; 6^4 ≡ 84 ≡ -17; 6^5 ≡ -102 ≡ -1. Hence 6^50 = (6^5)^10 ≡ 1. Also 101 = 4·24 + 5, so the result agrees with the rule.

(3) Test 2: is 6^33 ≡ 1 (mod 67)?
- 1 - 67 = -66 = -6·11, so 6^32 ≡ -11.
- -11 - 67 = -78 = -6·13, so 6^31 ≡ -13.
- -13 + 67 = 54 = 6·9, so 6^30 ≡ 9.
- [Implicit, mine:] 6^-3 = 6^30/6^33 ≡ 9 (indeed 6^3 ≡ 15 and 15·9 = 135 ≡ 1 mod 67).
Euler then descends by doubling steps:
- 6^27 = 6^30·6^-3 ≡ 81 ≡ 14.
- 6^21 = 6^27·6^-6 ≡ 14·14 = 196 ≡ -5.
- 6^9 = 6^21·6^-12 ≡ (-5)(-5) = 25.
- 6^3 = 6^9·6^-6 ≡ 25·14 = 350 ≡ 15.
- 6^0 = 6^3·6^-3 ≡ 15·9 = 135 ≡ 135 - 134 = 1.
The check is equivalent to 9^11 ≡ 1, i.e. 6^-33 ≡ 1, so it is a genuine verification. Also 67 = 3·24 - 5, which agrees with the rule.

(4) The table. For a = 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 11, Euler lists every odd residue class ±r (mod 4a) coprime to a. He states whether a prime 2p+1 in that class divides a^p - 1 (a is a quadratic residue) or a^p + 1 (a is a non-residue):
- a = 2: classes mod 8.
- a = 3: mod 12.
- a = 5: mod 20 (+ for ±1, ±9).
- a = 6: mod 24 (+ for ±1, ±5).
- a = 7: mod 28 (+ for ±1, ±3, ±9).
- a = 8: mod 32, effectively the mod 8 rule for 2.
- a = 10: mod 40 (+ for ±1, ±3, ±9, ±13).
- a = 11: mod 44 (+ for ±1, ±5, ±7, ±9, ±19).
In modern terms each entry asserts (a/q) = ±1 for q ≡ ±r (mod 4a). This is Euler's form of the law of quadratic reciprocity together with its supplementary law for 2.
errors: No arithmetic errors found. All residue steps in the mod 101 and mod 67 verifications check out.
Every one of the 42 sign entries in the table (a = 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 11) was checked against the Legendre symbol and is correct.

Logical remark: both verifications proceed by assuming the residue and reaching a consistent identity. Euler silently uses the assumption again to obtain 6^5 ≡ -1 and 6^-3 ≡ 9. Each check nevertheless reduces to a condition equivalent to the claim (e.g. 9^11 ≡ 1 mod 67), so it is valid.
The table rests on induction and empirical verification; no proof of the mod-4a dependence is given here.
The a = 8 table needlessly uses modulus 32, since the 2/8 character depends only on q mod 8.

results.what: For prime q = 2p+1 not dividing a, q divides exactly one of a^p - 1 or a^p + 1 according as a is or is not a quadratic residue mod q.
Which sign occurs depends only on q mod 4a, and is the same for q ≡ r and q ≡ -r (mod 4a). Explicit tables are given for a = 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 11.
results.modern_name: Quadratic reciprocity (Euler's 4a-formulation) with supplementary law for 2
results.usually_credited_to: Conjectured by Euler (E164 1751, E552 1783); Legendre 1785/1798; first proof Gauss 1796/1801

results.what: Computing or verifying a^k mod N by adding multiples of N to make the residue divisible by a, then dividing out powers of a to lower the exponent.
results.modern_name: Exact-division modular reduction (loosely analogous to Montgomery/Hensel-style reduction)
results.usually_credited_to: Euler's own computational device; the modern Montgomery reduction is from 1985

deep.surprise_reason: These are Euler's well-known empirical tables of quadratic characters mod 4a and his criterion. Both are standard and attributed to him (E164, E552), and this fragment was itself published in the Opera Posthuma (1862). The only mildly notable detail is his hand-computation trick of dividing out the base after adding multiples of the modulus.

checkable.asserts: the intermediate residues in the mod 67 verification (62 ≡ -5)

checkable.sympy: all(pow(6,(q-1)//2,q) == (1 if q%24 in (1,23,5,19) else q-1) for q in primerange(5,5000))
checkable.asserts: the a = 6 row of the table

checkable.sympy: all(legendre_symbol(5,q) == (1 if q%20 in (1,19,9,11) else -1) for q in primerange(7,5000))
all(legendre_symbol(7,q) == (1 if q%28 in (1,27,3,25,9,19) else -1) for q in primerange(3,5000) if q != 7)
all(legendre_symbol(10,q) == (1 if q%40 in (1,39,3,37,9,31,13,27) else -1) for q in primerange(7,5000))
all(legendre_symbol(11,q) == (1 if q%44 in (1,43,5,39,7,37,9,35,19,25) else -1) for q in primerange(3,5000) if q != 11)
all(legendre_symbol(8,q) == (1 if q%8 in (1,7) else -1) for q in primerange(3,5000))
checkable.asserts: the a = 8 row (depends only on q mod 8)
